name: Glasgow Municipal Cemetery
history: Municipal cemetery in Glasgow holding the grave of Confederate Brig. Gen. Joseph H. Lewis, commander of the First Kentucky (Orphan) Brigade. Lewis later served in Congress and as chief justice of the Kentucky Court of Appeals.

notable_burials.name: Joseph H. Lewis
notable_burials.significance: Commander of the Orphan Brigade; later Kentucky chief justice

name: Paris Cemetery
history: Incorporated in 1847 and NRHP-listed, Paris Cemetery is Bourbon County's principal historic burial ground with a notable gatehouse. It holds Bluegrass civic leaders and Civil War-era burials along South Main Street.

name: Bellevue Cemetery
history: Historic Danville cemetery adjacent to Danville National Cemetery. It holds Boyle County civic leaders and is part of the town's nineteenth-century burial landscape near Centre College.

name: Danville National Cemetery
history: Small Civil War national cemetery in Danville for Union soldiers who died in local hospitals. Administered by the VA and listed on the National Register, it is one of Kentucky's seven national cemeteries.

name: Mystery Cemetery
history: Small historic cemetery interpreted by a Kentucky Historical Society marker as the Mystery Cemetery, reflecting local research into poorly documented pioneer burials in Bullitt County. It is a visitor stop on the Shepherdsville heritage route.

name: Evergreen Cemetery
history: Major Northern Kentucky municipal cemetery serving Newport and Campbell County since the mid-nineteenth century. It is a well-known local historic landscape with Civil War and civic burials overlooking the Ohio River corridor.

name: East Broadway Cemetery
history: Public burial ground purchased by Winchester trustees in 1833 during the first cholera epidemic in the United States to reach the town. Seventy-five cholera victims were buried here that year, including trustee John Ward and his wife.

name: Hawes Family Cemetery
history: Family cemetery of Richard and Clary Walker Hawes, who settled here from Virginia in 1810. Their son Richard Hawes became Confederate governor of Kentucky; Clary later operated the Hawesville-Cannelton ferry.

notable_burials.name: Richard Hawes
notable_burials.significance: Early Daviess County settler; father of Confederate governor Richard Hawes

notable_burials.name: Clary Walker Hawes
notable_burials.significance: Ferry operator after her husband's death; family matriarch

name: Good Spring Baptist Church and Cemetery
history: NRHP-listed church and cemetery within Mammoth Cave National Park, representing nineteenth-century cave-country Baptist congregations. Visitors reach the quiet historic site on park roads near the Green River.

name: Joppa Baptist Church and Cemetery
history: Third of the NRHP-listed Baptist church-and-cemetery complexes preserved in Mammoth Cave National Park. Together with Good Spring and Mammoth Cave Baptist, it documents rural congregations of the cave region.

name: Mammoth Cave Baptist Church and Cemetery
history: Historic Baptist church and cemetery inside Mammoth Cave National Park, NRHP-listed with other park churchyards. It preserves the religious and burial landscape of the cave-country communities that predated the national park.

name: African Cemetery No. 2
history: Lexington's earliest recorded cemetery organized, owned, and managed by African Americans, founded by the Union Benevolent Society No. 2 in 1869. Leaders of Black fraternal, educational, and racing communities—and U.S. Colored Troops veterans—are buried here.

notable_burials.name: U.S. Colored Troops veterans
notable_burials.significance: Civil War soldiers interred among community leaders buried here

name: Episcopal Burying Ground and Chapel
history: Early Lexington Episcopal cemetery and Gothic chapel listed on the National Register. It is among the city's oldest surviving church burial grounds from the antebellum period; constitutional leader George Nicholas is associated with this historic burying ground.

notable_burials.name: George Nicholas
notable_burials.significance: First attorney general of Kentucky; early constitutional leader

name: Lexington Cemetery
history: Incorporated in 1849 as a naturalistic landscape park and arboretum, and NRHP-listed with the Henry Clay Monument. Notable Bluegrass burials include Henry Clay, Vice President John C. Breckinridge, Confederate cavalryman John Hunt Morgan, and author James Lane Allen.

notable_burials.name: Henry Clay
notable_burials.significance: Speaker of the House, senator, and Great Compromiser

notable_burials.name: John C. Breckinridge
notable_burials.significance: U.S. Vice President and Confederate major general

notable_burials.name: John Hunt Morgan
notable_burials.significance: Confederate cavalry general known as the Thunderbolt of the Confederacy

notable_burials.name: James Lane Allen
notable_burials.significance: Kentucky novelist of the Bluegrass

name: Lexington National Cemetery
history: Civil War national cemetery established in 1861 within Lexington Cemetery grounds for Union dead. It remains a VA-administered national cemetery and a quiet companion to the larger Victorian landscape park.

name: Elizaville Cemetery
history: Fleming County cemetery interpreted by KHS markers for World War II Marine hero Pfc. Franklin Sousley, one of the Iwo Jima flag raisers, who was later reinterred in Fleming County. It is a well-known eastern Kentucky memorial landscape.

notable_burials.name: Franklin Sousley
notable_burials.significance: Marine who helped raise the flag on Iwo Jima; later reinterred in Fleming County

name: Frankfort Cemetery
history: Hilltop rural cemetery overlooking the capital, incorporated in 1844 and NRHP-listed (74000872). Daniel and Rebecca Boone were reinterred here in 1845; nineteen Kentucky governors including William Goebel, Vice President Richard Mentor Johnson, and Marine hero Presley O'Bannon also rest on the bluff.

notable_burials.name: Daniel Boone
notable_burials.significance: Pioneer explorer; reinterred from Missouri in 1845

notable_burials.name: Rebecca Boone
notable_burials.significance: Pioneer settler and wife of Daniel Boone

notable_burials.name: Richard Mentor Johnson
notable_burials.significance: Ninth Vice President of the United States

notable_burials.name: William Goebel
notable_burials.significance: Only U.S. governor assassinated while in office

notable_burials.name: Presley O'Bannon
notable_burials.significance: Marine officer who raised the U.S. flag at Derna (Tripoli)

name: Frankfort State Hospital and School Cemetery
history: Burial ground associated with the Kentucky Institution for the Education and Training of Feeble-Minded Children (later Frankfort State Hospital and School). It documents institutionalized care and the anonymous dead of Kentucky's long-running state school hospital.

name: Greenhill Cemetery
history: Historic African American cemetery in Frankfort's Green Hill community, established after the Civil War. It holds the Kentucky African American Civil War Memorial (1924), the state's only monument honoring nearly 25,000 Kentuckians who served in the U.S. Colored Troops.

notable_burials.name: U.S. Colored Troops veterans
notable_burials.significance: Names of 142 Central Kentucky USCT men are etched on the 1924 memorial

name: Lancaster Cemetery
history: NRHP-listed municipal cemetery in Lancaster with significant nineteenth-century funerary architecture and Civil War-era burials. It is Garrard County's principal historic burial ground.

name: Helm Cemetery
history: Pioneer family cemetery with the graves of Governor John LaRue Helm and his son, Confederate Gen. Ben Hardin Helm, killed at Chickamauga. Ben Hardin Helm married Emilie Todd, half-sister of Mary Todd Lincoln, linking the plot to both Confederate and Lincoln family history.

notable_burials.name: John LaRue Helm
notable_burials.significance: Governor of Kentucky (two incomplete terms)

notable_burials.name: Benjamin Hardin Helm
notable_burials.significance: Confederate general; brother-in-law of Abraham Lincoln

name: The Old Cemetery (Cynthiana)
history: Only burial ground in Cynthiana from 1793 to 1868, on land deeded by town founder Robert Harrison. First mayor Samuel January and other early citizens are buried here; Harrison Academy once stood nearby.

notable_burials.name: Samuel January
notable_burials.significance: First mayor of Cynthiana

name: Fernwood Cemetery
history: Established in 1849; graves of Governor Lazarus W. Powell and Governor John Y. Brown, among other noted Kentuckians. Powell began the state's first geological survey to develop mineral and agricultural resources.

notable_burials.name: Lazarus W. Powell
notable_burials.significance: Governor of Kentucky (1851–55); initiated first state geological survey

notable_burials.name: John Y. Brown
notable_burials.significance: Governor of Kentucky and U.S. Representative

name: Berrytown Cemetery
history: Focal cemetery for the historic African American Berrytown community, which began when Alfred Berry purchased five acres in 1874. Purchased in 1890 by United Brothers of Friendship Lodge #83, which maintained the grounds and later built a lodge hall.

name: Cave Hill Cemetery
history: Louisville's premier Victorian garden cemetery and arboretum, chartered in 1848 and listed on the National Register in 1979. It holds the graves of Louisville founder George Rogers Clark, Muhammad Ali, and Colonel Harland Sanders, plus Union and Confederate Civil War burials including Cave Hill National Cemetery within its grounds.

notable_burials.name: George Rogers Clark
notable_burials.significance: Revolutionary War general and founder of Louisville

notable_burials.name: Muhammad Ali
notable_burials.significance: Boxing champion and Louisville native

notable_burials.name: Harland Sanders
notable_burials.significance: Founder of Kentucky Fried Chicken

notable_burials.name: Patty Hill
notable_burials.significance: Co-composer of the melody for Happy Birthday to You

name: Cave Hill National Cemetery
history: Civil War-era national cemetery inside Cave Hill, with Union dead from Louisville hospitals and camps and later concentrated burials including USCT soldiers. Administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs and listed on the National Register with other Civil War national cemeteries.

name: Eastern Cemetery
history: Fifteen acres incorporated in 1854 for the Methodist Episcopal Church; later home to Kentucky's first crematorium (1935). Abandoned after overburial scandals were exposed in 1989, it is a cautionary landmark of cemetery mismanagement beside Cave Hill.

name: Forest Home Cemetery
history: Evolved from an old slave burial ground and is the resting place of Eliza Curtis Hundley Tevis and other early settlers of the Petersburg community. Tevis was born enslaved, gained freedom in 1833, and with her husband Henry purchased land that anchored the free Black settlement.

notable_burials.name: Eliza Curtis Hundley Tevis
notable_burials.significance: Formerly enslaved settler who helped found Petersburg

name: Long Run Baptist Church and Cemetery
history: Pioneer Baptist church and cemetery associated with early Jefferson County settlement and Long Run Massacre memory. The church-and-cemetery complex is listed on the National Register as a frontier religious landscape east of Louisville.

name: Louisville Cemetery
history: African American cemetery incorporated in 1886 by prominent Black citizens including Bishop W. H. Miles. Burials include Dr. Robert B. Scott, cofounder of Louisville Red Cross Hospital, and other educators and community leaders.

notable_burials.name: Robert B. Scott
notable_burials.significance: Physician; cofounder of Louisville Red Cross Hospital

name: Pennsylvania Run Presbyterian Church and Cemetery
history: Started by Presbyterian families who came from Pennsylvania to Kentucky in the 1780s; first log church in the 1790s and present brick church in 1840. One of the oldest surviving Presbyterian church-and-cemetery complexes in Jefferson County.

name: Zachary Taylor National Cemetery
history: National cemetery on the old Taylor family burial ground at Springfield, named for the twelfth U.S. president. Zachary Taylor and Margaret Taylor rest in a limestone mausoleum; the site also holds Revolutionary War colonel Richard Taylor and later veterans of twentieth-century wars.

notable_burials.name: Zachary Taylor
notable_burials.significance: Twelfth President of the United States; Mexican War general

notable_burials.name: Margaret Mackall Smith Taylor
notable_burials.significance: First Lady of the United States

notable_burials.name: Richard Taylor
notable_burials.significance: Revolutionary War officer and father of Zachary Taylor

name: Camp Nelson National Cemetery
history: One of the original Civil War national cemeteries, tied to Camp Nelson's Union supply depot, hospital, and major U.S. Colored Troops recruitment center. More than a thousand wartime dead were buried here by 1866; the cemetery remains an active VA national cemetery beside Camp Nelson National Monument.

name: Highland Cemetery
history: Premier rural garden cemetery of northern Kentucky, planned by landscape architect Adolph Strauch and NRHP-listed as a historic district (89001585). It is known for Confederate and Union veterans, civic leaders, and finely designed monuments and mausoleums; members of the Goebel family (not Governor William Goebel himself) are among those interred here.

name: Linden Grove Cemetery
history: Founded in 1843 on land of the Western Baptist Theological Institute; final resting place of veterans since the War of 1812. The cemetery and its GAR monuments are listed on the National Register and interpret Covington's nineteenth-century civic history.

name: Isaac Shelby Cemetery State Historic Site
history: Final resting place of Isaac Shelby, Kentucky's first and fifth governor and a Revolutionary War leader, at his Traveler's Rest plantation. The small Kentucky State Historic Site near Junction City interprets Shelby's frontier and early-statehood career.

notable_burials.name: Isaac Shelby
notable_burials.significance: First and fifth governor of Kentucky; Revolutionary War officer

name: John Littlejohn Cemetery
history: Burial place associated with Methodist circuit rider John Littlejohn, a noted early Kentucky preacher. The KHS-marked cemetery interprets frontier religious life in the Logan County / Russellville area.

notable_burials.name: John Littlejohn
notable_burials.significance: Methodist circuit rider and early Kentucky preacher

name: Red River Presbyterian Meetinghouse Site and Cemetery
history: NRHP-listed site of the Red River Meeting House, cradle of the Great Revival / Second Great Awakening camp-meeting movement in Kentucky (1800). The adjacent cemetery marks the Presbyterian frontier congregation that hosted the historic meetings.

name: Matthew Lyon Grave
history: Grave of Matthew Lyon, Revolutionary War soldier, Vermont congressman prosecuted under the Alien and Sedition Acts, and later western Kentucky settler. Lyon County takes its name from him; the KHS marker interprets his national and Kentucky significance.

notable_burials.name: Matthew Lyon
notable_burials.significance: Congressman; namesake of Lyon County; Alien and Sedition Acts defendant

name: Richmond Cemetery
history: Principal historic cemetery for Richmond and Madison County, with Civil War-era and civic burials. Emancipationist Cassius Marcellus Clay, Lincoln's minister to Russia, is buried in the Richmond area commemorative landscape interpreted by a nearby KHS marker.

notable_burials.name: Cassius Marcellus Clay
notable_burials.significance: Emancipationist publisher; U.S. minister to Russia

name: Lebanon National Cemetery
history: Civil War national cemetery outside Lebanon for Union dead from the 1862–63 campaigns in Central Kentucky. It remains a VA national cemetery and NRHP-listed Civil War burial ground.

name: Mount Kenton Cemetery
history: Historic Paducah cemetery best known as the burial place of author and humorist Irvin S. Cobb. A KHS marker interprets Cobb's career and interment at Mount Kenton.

notable_burials.name: Irvin S. Cobb
notable_burials.significance: Paducah-born author, humorist, and journalist

name: New Providence Presbyterian Cemetery
history: Pioneer Presbyterian church cemetery near McAfee in Mercer County, noted on a KHS marker for Revolutionary War soldiers buried at New Providence. It represents early settlement faith communities in the Harrodsburg hinterland.

name: Old Fort Harrod Pioneer Cemetery
history: Pioneer burial ground at Old Fort Harrod State Park, interpreting Kentucky's first permanent settlement (1774). The cemetery and reconstructed fort tell the story of early Bluegrass frontier life at Harrodsburg.

name: Old Mulkey Meetinghouse Cemetery
history: Pioneer Baptist cemetery beside the 1804 log Old Mulkey Meetinghouse, among Kentucky's oldest surviving meetinghouses. The state historic site preserves frontier graves—including Hannah Boone Pennington, sister of Daniel Boone—and early Baptist worship traditions.

notable_burials.name: Hannah Boone Pennington
notable_burials.significance: Sister of Daniel Boone, associated with the pioneer congregation

name: Tompkinsville National Cemetery
history: Civil War burial ground for Union soldiers who died in the Tompkinsville region; most remains were moved to Nashville National Cemetery in 1867, leaving a tiny remnant national cemetery. A KHS marker interprets the site's wartime role and later reduction.

name: Machpelah Cemetery
history: NRHP-listed cemetery in Mount Sterling known for its collection of cast-iron fences and nineteenth-century monuments. It is Montgomery County's principal historic burial landscape.

name: Old Greenville Cemetery
history: Land given to the Presbyterian Church by Charles and Nancy Wing in 1825–26; later deeded to the city. Distinguished War of 1812 rifleman Ephraim M. Brank—later celebrated in historical fiction—is among those buried here.

notable_burials.name: Ephraim M. Brank
notable_burials.significance: War of 1812 marksman later memorialized in Kentucky lore

name: Pewee Valley Confederate Cemetery
history: NRHP-listed cemetery associated with the Kentucky Confederate Home (1902–1934). A granite obelisk marks the graves of hundreds of Confederate veterans who died as residents of the home—a rare public Confederate veterans landscape in the Louisville ring counties.

name: McCoy Cemetery
history: Family cemetery central to Hatfield-McCoy feud memory. Among those buried here are Randolph McCoy's sons Tolbert, Pharmer, and Randolph Jr., and Alifair and Calvin McCoy, killed when the family cabin was burned—part of the Hatfield-McCoy Historic District story.

notable_burials.name: Tolbert McCoy
notable_burials.significance: Son of Randolph McCoy; killed during the Hatfield-McCoy feud

notable_burials.name: Alifair McCoy
notable_burials.significance: Daughter of Randolph McCoy; killed in the New Year 1888 cabin attack

notable_burials.name: Calvin McCoy
notable_burials.significance: Son of Randolph McCoy; killed in the New Year 1888 cabin attack

name: Mill Springs National Cemetery
history: National cemetery near the Mill Springs battlefield, where Union forces won a critical early Civil War victory in January 1862. It holds wartime dead from the campaign and later veterans, adjacent to Mill Springs Battlefield National Monument.

name: Georgetown Cemetery
history: Incorporated in 1850; older stones reflect reinterments from earlier graveyards. Governors Joseph Desha and James F. Robinson, Confederate governor George W. Johnson, and equine artist Edward Troye are among those buried here.

notable_burials.name: Joseph Desha
notable_burials.significance: Ninth governor of Kentucky

notable_burials.name: James F. Robinson
notable_burials.significance: Civil War-era governor of Kentucky

notable_burials.name: George W. Johnson
notable_burials.significance: First Confederate governor of Kentucky

notable_burials.name: Edward Troye
notable_burials.significance: Noted equine portrait painter

name: Grove Hill Cemetery
history: Shelbyville's historic park cemetery overlooking Clear Creek, with burials from 1855 onward and a National Register-listed chapel. Revolutionary War heroes Col. John S. Hardin and Aquilla Whitaker are commemorated here, along with Civil War Union lots donated to the War Department.

notable_burials.name: Aquilla Whitaker
notable_burials.significance: Revolutionary War veteran; helped lay out Shelbyville and the Midland Trail

notable_burials.name: John S. Hardin
notable_burials.significance: Revolutionary War officer commemorated with a cenotaph at Grove Hill

name: Elk Creek Cemetery (James Morrison Heady)
history: Rural Spencer County cemetery at Elk Creek associated with James Morrison Heady, the Blind Bard of Kentucky, who was blind by fifteen and deaf before forty yet invented assistive devices and wrote widely. A short drive from Shelby/Bagdad for eastern Jefferson-Spencer heritage trips.

notable_burials.name: James Morrison Heady
notable_burials.significance: Blind and deaf inventor and author known as the Blind Bard of Kentucky

name: Fairview Cemetery
history: Bowling Green's main historic cemetery, resting place of Confederate operative Capt. Thomas H. Hines—called one of the most dangerous men of the Confederacy—and other Warren County leaders. A KHS marker interprets Hines's wartime career and burial here.

notable_burials.name: Thomas H. Hines
notable_burials.significance: Confederate officer; Kentucky Court of Appeals judge

name: Sons & Daughters of Relief Cemetery
history: Land bought in 1876 by members of Midway's Sons & Daughters of Relief lodge. Final resting place of veterans and formerly enslaved leaders of Midway's African American community, including famous horseman Edward Dudley Brown in an unmarked grave.

notable_burials.name: Edward Dudley Brown
notable_burials.significance: Formerly enslaved Thoroughbred trainer and jockey (Brown Dick)
